warmup.q: A pipeline reads supplyAsync(this::grill, kitchen).thenApply(this::addSauce).thenApply(this::plate).exceptionally(ex -> apology). grill throws an IllegalStateException. What happens?
options: addSauce and plate run with a null steak
addSauce and plate are skipped, and exceptionally gets the exception wrapped in a CompletionException
supplyAsync throws the exception on the calling thread
addSauce and plate are skipped, and exceptionally gets the IllegalStateException itself
warmup.why: A failed stage skips every later thenApply until a handler. The handler gets a CompletionException with the IllegalStateException as its cause, because the exception was thrown inside a stage. The last option is the tempting one, and code that checks ex instanceof IllegalStateException there is quietly wrong. The first two sections show both halves.

opening:
Last lesson, the ticket for table 4 carried its own instructions: when the steak and the sauce are ready, plate them. In code, that ticket was a CompletableFuture, a promise of a result that starts the next step by itself.

Now the steak burns. The sauce cook has no business pouring sauce on charcoal, so a note goes on the ticket instead: "burned at the grill". Every later station passes the ticket along untouched, until someone at the pass, the counter where dishes leave the kitchen, reads the note and decides what table 4 gets.

CompletableFuture handles failure the same way, with three surprises. The note sometimes arrives in an envelope. A timer that tells the manager to stop waiting doesn't stop the cook. And waiting for three dishes at once fails the whole table when one of them burns. All three pass a quick test, because tests rarely burn the steak.

In this lesson, we'll follow a failure down a pipeline, open the envelope and put deadlines on slow calls. Then we'll ask three suppliers for a price without letting one bad answer spoil the rest. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a steak that burned at the grill. Its note skipped every station on the way to the pass, sometimes in an envelope. The kitchen timer freed the manager while the cook stayed on hold. And three suppliers gave one price, once no call could spoil the errand.

Now search your own code for orTimeout(, and check that the call underneath has a timeout of its own. Then search for allOf(, and make sure every future it waits for has its own deadline and handler.

Next, we'll go back to the chopping board, where the work is all arithmetic. How does a ForkJoinPool keep every cook busy on one big job, with no manager handing out tickets?

sections.h: A dish burns at the grill: how a failure skips every step until a handler
sections.html:
Let's put the kitchen into code. A future is a claim ticket for a result that isn't ready yet, and a CompletableFuture is one you can attach the next step to. A stage is one such step, such as a thenApply, that runs when the step before it has finished. Our grill runs on kitchen, a thread pool: a few threads, paths of work that run side by side, taking tasks from one queue. Three plain stages follow the grill, one per station. Then come two handlers, which we'll meet in a moment:

Java
CompletableFuture<String> result = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(ErrorPathDemo::grill, kitchen)
        .thenApply(s -> step("1. pour the sauce on " + s, s + " with pepper sauce"))
        .thenApply(s -> step("2. plate " + s, "a plate of " + s))
        .thenApply(s -> step("3. carry it to table 4", "table 4 got " + s))
        .whenComplete((v, ex) -> System.out.println("whenComplete sees: " + (ex == null ? v : ex)))
        .exceptionally(ex -> {                              // the pass
            System.out.println("exceptionally sees: " + ex);
            return "table 4 got an apology and the menu";
        });
Kotlin
val result = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::grill, kitchen)
    .thenApply { s -> step("1. pour the sauce on $s", "$s with pepper sauce") }
    .thenApply { s -> step("2. plate $s", "a plate of $s") }
    .thenApply { s -> step("3. carry it to table 4", "table 4 got $s") }
    .whenComplete { v, ex -> println("whenComplete sees: ${ex ?: v}") }
    .exceptionally { ex ->                                  // the pass
        println("exceptionally sees: $ex")
        "table 4 got an apology and the menu"
    }

step prints its text and returns the value, so we can see which stations did any work. And grill always throws an IllegalStateException that says the steak burned. Before you read on, decide which numbered lines will print.

ErrorPathDemo, in the Try it below, printed this:

whenComplete sees: java.util.concurrent.CompletionException: java.lang.IllegalStateException: the steak burned
exceptionally sees: java.util.concurrent.CompletionException: java.lang.IllegalStateException: the steak burned
result: table 4 got an apology and the menu

Not one numbered line. When a stage throws, its future completes exceptionally: it finishes with an exception instead of a value. Every thenApply, thenCompose and thenCombine after it is then skipped. Its function never runs, and its own future fails with the same cause. That's the note on the ticket, passed from station to station.

The failure stops at the first handler, a stage that also runs when the step before it failed. There are four:

Method Runs on Changes the outcome?
exceptionally(ex -> value) failure only yes, replaces the failure with a value
handle((value, ex) -> result) success and failure yes, returns any result
whenComplete((value, ex) -> ...) success and failure no, passes the outcome on
exceptionallyCompose(ex -> future) failure only yes, with another future (JDK 12)

whenComplete is the manager who glances at every ticket on its way past and writes in the log. It sees both outcomes and hands the same one on, so it suits logs and counters. (One detail: if its own action throws after a success, the result becomes that new failure. After a failure, the original failure wins.) exceptionally is the pass. It replaces the failure with a value, and everything after it sees a success.

Where you put the handler decides what you can still save. At the end, after the sauce, the plate and the walk to table 4 were all skipped, the only honest thing left is an apology. Move the handler up, right after the grill, and it can swap in a spare steak. Then every station after it works as if nothing had gone wrong. Run the demo with early, and it prints:

exceptionally sees: java.util.concurrent.CompletionException: java.lang.IllegalStateException: the steak burned
1. pour the sauce on the spare steak
2. plate the spare steak with pepper sauce
3. carry it to table 4
whenComplete sees: table 4 got a plate of the spare steak with pepper sauce

Recover as close to the failure as you can. Every step after the handler then runs as usual.

Sometimes the fallback takes time of its own. Cooking a new steak on the second grill returns a future, not a steak. For that case, use exceptionallyCompose, added in JDK 12 (version 12 of Java's development kit). It is to exceptionally what thenCompose is to thenApply:

Java
CompletableFuture<String> steak = grill.cookAsync(order)
        .exceptionallyCompose(ex -> spareGrill.cookAsync(order));   // JDK 12+: the fallback is a future too
Kotlin
val steak: CompletableFuture<String> = grill.cookAsync(order)
    .exceptionallyCompose { spareGrill.cookAsync(order) }          // JDK 12+: the fallback is a future too

Look again at what our two handlers printed, though. They didn't get our IllegalStateException. They got a CompletionException with ours inside, like a note sealed in an envelope. Where did the envelope come from?

try.title: Move the handler
steps: Run ErrorPathDemo. The grill throws. Before you run it, write down which of the numbered steps will print.
Run it with -Pargs=early, which recovers right after the grill. Predict again, including what whenComplete sees.

code.title: ErrorPathDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l07; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** The steak burns at the grill. Which steps still run? Pass "early" to recover right after the grill. */ public class ErrorPathDemo { static String grill() { throw new IllegalStateException("the steak burned"); } static <T> T step(String what, T value) { System.out.println(what); return value; } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean early = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("early"); try (ExecutorService kitchen = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("cook-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<String> steak = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(ErrorPathDemo::grill, kitchen); if (early) { steak = steak.exceptionally(ex -> { // recover the steak itself System.out.println("exceptionally sees: " + ex); return "the spare steak"; // kept warm for nights like this }); } CompletableFuture<String> result = steak .thenApply(s -> step("1. pour the sauce on " + s, s + " with pepper sauce")) .thenApply(s -> step("2. plate " + s, "a plate of " + s)) .thenApply(s -> step("3. carry it to table 4", "table 4 got " + s)) .whenComplete((v, ex) -> System.out.println("whenComplete sees: " + (ex == null ? v : ex))); if (!early) { result = result.exceptionally(ex -> { // recover at the pass instead System.out.println("exceptionally sees: " + ex); return "table 4 got an apology and the menu"; }); } System.out.println("result: " + result.join()); } } }

With early, exceptionally runs first and returns the spare steak, then steps 1, 2 and 3 run, and whenComplete sees a success: table 4 got a plate of the spare steak with pepper sauce.

video.title: A failure skips every stage until a handler catches it, orTimeout fills the future but leaves the call running, and a handle on each call keeps one bad answer from failing allOf

sections.h: The note in an envelope: when a handler gets CompletionException, and when it doesn't
sections.html:
Handlers don't always get your exception. They get one of two things, by a rule that surprises everyone once.

A CompletionException is an unchecked exception, one that Java doesn't make you catch, that CompletableFuture wraps around a failure, with your exception inside as its cause. It's the envelope.

If the exception was thrown inside a stage, by a supplyAsync task or a thenApply function, the future stores it in an envelope. A handler on that future, or on any later stage, gets the CompletionException, and getCause() returns your exception. That's what our burned steak did.

If somebody completed the future by hand, with completeExceptionally(ex), the future stores ex just as it is. orTimeout, which the next section covers, works that way, and so do many libraries that hand you a future. A handler attached right to that future gets the bare exception. One stage later it's in an envelope again, because the failure crossed a stage boundary on its way.

WrapDemo prints every case. Cover the output below, and predict each line before you read it:

1. handle() on the supplyAsync future      CompletionException <- IllegalStateException
2. handle() on completeExceptionally       IllegalStateException
3. handle() one stage later                CompletionException <- IllegalStateException
4. handle() after orTimeout                TimeoutException
5. get() throws                            ExecutionException <- IllegalStateException
6. join() throws                           CompletionException <- IllegalStateException

Lines 2 and 4 are bare, because someone completed those futures by hand. The last two lines are the blocking calls from the last lesson, the ones that make a thread wait for the result: get() throws ExecutionException and join() throws CompletionException, both with the original exception as the cause.

So a handler that checks ex instanceof TimeoutException can be right in one place and quietly wrong one stage further down. Open the envelope first, then decide:

Java
.exceptionally(ex -> {
    Throwable cause = (ex instanceof CompletionException && ex.getCause() != null) ? ex.getCause() : ex;
    if (cause instanceof TimeoutException) return lastWeeksPrice;
    throw new CompletionException(cause);       // not ours to handle: keep failing
})
Kotlin
.exceptionally { ex ->
    val cause = if (ex is CompletionException && ex.cause != null) ex.cause!! else ex
    if (cause is TimeoutException) lastWeeksPrice
    else throw CompletionException(cause)       // not ours to handle: keep failing
}

First we take the cause out, if there is an envelope. Then we handle the one case we know, a timeout, with last week's price. The last line reads as "I opened it, and this one isn't mine, so pass it on." Throwing inside a handler keeps the future failing, so a later handler, or the caller, can deal with it.

The lab's unwrap method does the same job in a loop. It also strips the ExecutionException that get() adds, in case one wrapper ends up inside another. And on a future you know has failed, exceptionNow() (JDK 19) hands you the exception with the envelope already removed.

Open the envelope before you test the type. Rethrow what isn't yours.

Line 4 of the demo came from a timeout. A timeout looks like the cure for a slow call. It is only half of one.

try.title: Predict the envelope
steps: Cover the output in the section. Read WrapDemo and write down, for each numbered line, what you expect it to print.
Run it and check. For each line you got wrong, find out whether the exception was thrown inside a stage or passed to completeExceptionally.

code.title: WrapDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l07; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Which exception does each handler see? Predict every line before you run it. */ public class WrapDemo { static String describe(Throwable ex) { String name = ex.getClass().getSimpleName(); return ex.getCause() == null ? name : name + " <- " + ex.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName(); } static void show(String label, CompletableFuture<?> f) { String seen = f.handle((v, ex) -> describe(ex)).join(); System.out.printf("%-42s %s%n", label, seen); } public static void main(String[] args) { IllegalStateException down = new IllegalStateException("the steak burned"); try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<String> supplied = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { throw down; }, io); CompletableFuture<String> completed = new CompletableFuture<>(); completed.completeExceptionally(down); CompletableFuture<String> timedOut = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> sleepThen(1000, "late"), io) .orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); show("1. handle() on the supplyAsync future", supplied); show("2. handle() on completeExceptionally", completed); show("3. handle() one stage later", completed.thenApply(String::trim)); show("4. handle() after orTimeout", timedOut); try { supplied.get(); } catch (ExecutionException | InterruptedException e) { System.out.printf("%-42s %s%n", "5. get() throws", describe(e)); } try { supplied.join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { System.out.printf("%-42s %s%n", "6. join() throws", describe(e)); } } } static String sleepThen(long ms, String value) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return value; } }

Predict every line before you run it. */ fun main() { val down = IllegalStateException("the steak burned") Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> val supplied = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync<String>({ throw down }, io) val completed = CompletableFuture<String>() completed.completeExceptionally(down) val timedOut = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ Thread.sleep(1000); "late" }, io) .orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) show("1. handle() on the supplyAsync future", supplied) show("2. handle() on completeExceptionally", completed) show("3. handle() one stage later", completed.thenApply { it.trim() }) show("4. handle() after orTimeout", timedOut) try { supplied.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { println("%-42s %s".format("5. get() throws", describe(e))) } try { supplied.join() } catch (e: CompletionException) { println("%-42s %s".format("6. join() throws", describe(e))) } } }

try.expect: The six lines shown in the section. Lines 2 and 4 are bare exceptions, because completeExceptionally and orTimeout store them as they are. Every exception that was thrown inside a stage, or crossed one on its way, arrives as a CompletionException.

sections.h: A kitchen timer for the manager: orTimeout ends the wait, not the work
sections.html:
Timeouts need a scene of their own. The restaurant buys flour from a few suppliers, and each supplier has a web service: a program on another computer that answers questions over the network. Ask it for today's price of a sack of flour, and it answers within a few hundred milliseconds. On a bad day, it doesn't answer at all.

In code, asking is a blocking call. It holds a thread until the answer comes, just like the slow web service from Sizing a pool. So picture the call as a cook on the phone to the supplier. The manager wants the price, so he starts a kitchen timer. When it rings, he stops waiting and decides without it. Nobody tells the cook, who stays on hold, listening to the supplier's music.

JDK 9 gave CompletableFuture two such kitchen timers:

Java
price.orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);                       // fails with TimeoutException
price.completeOnTimeout(lastWeeksPrice, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);  // completes with a default
Kotlin
price.orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)                        // fails with TimeoutException
price.completeOnTimeout(lastWeeksPrice, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)   // completes with a default

Both change the future you call them on, and return it. If the future hasn't completed when the time is up, a timer thread inside the JDK completes it: orTimeout with a TimeoutException, completeOnTimeout with the value you gave it. The thread's name depends on the JDK. On JDK 21 it's CompletableFutureDelayScheduler, and on JDK 25 it's ForkJoinPool.commonPool-delayScheduler. Plain stages attached to the future, the ones without Async in their name, then run on that thread, so keep them cheap.

Now the trap. Neither timer touches the call. KeepsRunningDemo gives a 600 ms call to a slow supplier a deadline of 200 ms. On JDK 21 it printed this:

  36 ms  io-1                                   asking the slow supplier for a price
 236 ms  CompletableFutureDelayScheduler        the future completed with TimeoutException
 695 ms  io-1                                   the supplier answered, but nobody is listening
 702 ms  main                                   pool closed

The future failed right on time. The call finished anyway, about 600 ms after it started, holding io-1 the whole way, and the pool's close() had to wait for it. The answer went nowhere.

Maybe cancel(true) can hang up the phone? Run the demo with cancel:

 243 ms  main                                   cancel(true) returned true
 247 ms  main                                   the future completed with CancellationException
 773 ms  io-1                                   the supplier answered, but nobody is listening

As far as the future knows, the cancel worked. The line interrupted: the call stops here never printed, though, so the call never noticed. The CompletableFuture Javadoc, its official documentation, says the flag mayInterruptIfRunning "has no effect in this implementation because interrupts are not used to control processing."

The source code shows why. supplyAsync hands the pool a small task that points to the future. The future keeps no pointer back to that task, or to the thread that runs it. So cancel can only store a CancellationException as the result. There's no thread it could interrupt.

The FutureTask that submit returns is the opposite. Its cancel(true) sends an interrupt, the polite request to stop from Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption.

Here the kitchen picture breaks. A real manager could walk over and tell the cook to hang up. A CompletableFuture has no line back to its cook at all.

Under load, that is how a pool fills up with nothing. Take a pool of 20 threads and a supplier that hangs for 30 seconds. Every request gets its TimeoutException after 300 ms, right on time. But every call holds its thread for 30 seconds. After 20 requests, all 20 cooks are on hold. New calls, even to healthy suppliers, wait in the pool's queue behind them and time out too.

So every call to another computer needs two timeouts. The one on the future is the caller's deadline. The one inside the client makes the call itself give up, and that gives the thread back. Java's HTTP client, the JDK's own tool for calling web services, takes it on the request:

Java
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri)
        .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300))    // the call itself gives up after 300 ms
        .build();
Kotlin
val request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri)
    .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300))        // the call itself gives up after 300 ms
    .build()

Set the client's timeout no longer than the future's. And give each supplier a limit of its own, a bulkhead from Sizing a pool, so one hung supplier can't take every thread. (A bulkhead is a separate cap on calls to each slow service.)

A timeout on the future frees the caller, not the thread. Give the call its own timeout too.

One call with a deadline is under control now. But the manager doesn't want one price. He wants three, and he wants them at the same time.

try.title: Time out a call, then watch it finish
steps: Run KeepsRunningDemo. Read the thread names and the timestamps.
Run it with -Pargs=cancel, which calls cancel(true) at 200 ms instead. Predict first: does the call see an interrupt?

code.title: KeepsRunningDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l07; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** A 600 ms call to a slow supplier with orTimeout(200 ms). Pass "cancel" to try cancel(true) at 200 ms instead. */ public class KeepsRunningDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %-38s %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().getName(), msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean cancel = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("cancel"); try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> quote = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { log("asking the slow supplier for a price"); try { Thread.sleep(600); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("interrupted: the call stops here"); throw new IllegalStateException(e); } log("the supplier answered, but nobody is listening"); return new BigDecimal("19.80"); }, io); if (cancel) { Thread.sleep(200); log("cancel(true) returned " + quote.cancel(true)); } else { quote.orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } quote.handle((v, ex) -> { log("the future completed with " + (ex == null ? v : ex.getClass().getSimpleName())); return null; }).join(); } // close() waits for the supplier call, which is still running log("pool closed"); } }

Pass "cancel" to try cancel(true) at 200 ms instead. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val cancel = args.firstOrNull() == "cancel" Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> val quote = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ log("asking the slow supplier for a price") try { Thread.sleep(600) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("interrupted: the call stops here") throw IllegalStateException(e) } log("the supplier answered, but nobody is listening") BigDecimal("19.80") }, io) if (cancel) { Thread.sleep(200) log("cancel(true) returned ${quote.cancel(true)}") } else { quote.orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) } quote.handle { v, ex -> log("the future completed with ${if (ex == null) v else ex.javaClass.simpleName}") }.join() } // close() waits for the supplier call, which is still running log("pool closed") }

try.expect: The future completes with TimeoutException at about 200 ms, on the timer thread (CompletableFutureDelayScheduler on JDK 21, ForkJoinPool.commonPool-delayScheduler on JDK 25). The supplier still answers at about 600 ms, and pool closed waits for it. With cancel, cancel(true) returns true and the future completes with CancellationException on main, but the line interrupted never prints: the call runs to the end.

aside.title: Does a framework's timeout stop the work?
aside.html: If you write web services, your framework or a fault-tolerance library may let you put a timeout on a method with an annotation, often called @Timeout. Ask it the same question as orTimeout: when the time is up, does only the wait end, or does the work stop too? Some tools run the method on another thread and simply stop waiting for it. Others also interrupt that thread, which stops the call only if the call responds to interrupts. Either way, the client's own timeout is what reliably gives the thread back.

sections.h: Three suppliers at once: allOf, anyOf, and one bad answer that mustn't spoil the rest
sections.html:
Back to the flour. Three suppliers sell it: the corner shop, the market and the mill. The manager wants today's price from all three, and he'll buy from the cheapest. Phoning them one after another wastes time, so three cooks phone at once. Sending out several calls at the same time and collecting the answers is called a fan-out. In code, it's three futures, all started before we wait for any of them.

FanOutDemo sets up the three suppliers with delays chosen for teaching. The corner shop fails after 50 ms, because it's closed today. The market answers 21.50 after 100 ms, and the mill answers 19.80 after 300 ms. The JDK has two methods that combine many futures, and the demo tries both.

allOf(f1, f2, f3) returns a CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when all three have completed. It carries no results of its own. You read them from your own futures with join(), which no longer blocks, because they're all done. Predict what -Pargs=all prints, then compare:

  84 ms  corner fails
 151 ms  market answers 21.50
 333 ms  mill answers 19.80
 336 ms  all: failed with java.lang.IllegalStateException: corner is closed today

Two good prices came back, and the errand failed anyway. If any of its futures fails, allOf fails too, and only after the slowest one has finished. (Every timestamp runs a little late, because the clock starts before the pool does, and the machine was busy with other work.)

anyOf(f1, f2, f3) returns a future that completes the same way as the first of them to finish. Here's -Pargs=any:

  99 ms  corner fails
 161 ms  any: failed with java.lang.IllegalStateException: corner is closed today
 161 ms  market answers 21.50
 352 ms  mill answers 19.80

The corner shop answered first, with the worst possible news, and anyOf took it. The first to finish includes failures. If you want the first successful answer, anyOf can't give it to you. (Go deeper has a ten-line helper for that.)

So neither method does the errand on its own. The fix is to make each call unable to fail before we combine them. Give every call its own deadline, then turn any failure into "no answer":

Java
CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>> safe = ask(supplier)
        .orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)                       // this supplier's deadline
        .handle((price, ex) -> ex == null ? Optional.of(price) : Optional.empty());
Kotlin
val safe: CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>> = ask(supplier)
    .orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)                          // this supplier's deadline
    .handle { price, ex -> if (ex == null) Optional.of(price) else Optional.empty() }

handle sees both outcomes and returns a new result either way: the price inside an Optional, or an empty Optional. Now allOf over the safe futures can only succeed, and the step after it picks the lowest price that came back. Here's -Pargs=safe:

  91 ms  corner fails
 170 ms  market answers 21.50
 340 ms  mill answers 19.80
 353 ms  safe: result 19.80

That's the mill's price, the cheapest, from the slowest supplier. The closed corner shop turned into an empty Optional, and it spoiled nothing.

The deadline must sit on each call. Put one orTimeout on the allOf instead, and a single hung supplier throws away the two good answers.

Make each call unable to fail before you combine them. Then pick from what came back.

That's the lab. Its QuoteAggregator asks every supplier for a quote, a price offer, all at the same time. Each call gets its own deadline, every skipped supplier is reported with its real cause, and the lowest price wins.

Notice the limit of the tool before we leave the phones. A CompletableFuture is good at waiting for calls and combining their answers. It can't stop a call it gave up on, and when one call fails, it doesn't cancel the others. It was built for work that waits. For work that is all arithmetic, the JDK has a pool of its own.

try.title: Three ways to fan out
steps: Read FanOutDemo: the corner shop fails at 50 ms, the market answers at 100 ms, the mill at 300 ms.
Run it with -Pargs=any, then -Pargs=all, then -Pargs=safe. Before each run, predict the result and when it arrives.

code.title: FanOutDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l07; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.Optional; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** Three suppliers quote a sack of flour: corner fails at 50 ms, market answers at 100 ms, mill at 300 ms. Pass any, all or safe. */ public class FanOutDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> ask(String name, long ms, String price, ExecutorService io) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { sleep(ms); if (price == null) { log(name + " fails"); throw new IllegalStateException(name + " is closed today"); } log(name + " answers " + price); return new BigDecimal(price); }, io); } public static void main(String[] args) { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "all"; try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { List<CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>> asks = List.of( ask("corner", 50, null, io), ask("market", 100, "21.50", io), ask("mill", 300, "19.80", io)); CompletableFuture<?> result = switch (mode) { // the first future to complete wins, even when it completes with a failure case "any" -> CompletableFuture.anyOf(asks.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)); // waits for all three, then fails because one of them failed case "all" -> CompletableFuture.allOf(asks.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) .thenApply(done -> asks.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).min(Comparator.naturalOrder()).orElseThrow()); // turn each failure into an empty Optional first, so allOf can't fail default -> { List<CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>>> safe = asks.stream() .map(f -> f.handle((price, ex) -> ex == null ? Optional.of(price) : Optional.<BigDecimal>empty())) .toList(); yield CompletableFuture.allOf(safe.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) .thenApply(done -> safe.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).flatMap(Optional::stream) .min(Comparator.naturalOrder()).orElseThrow()); } }; result.handle((v, ex) -> { log(mode + ": " + (ex == null ? "result " + v : "failed with " + ex.getCause())); return null; }).join(); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: FanOutDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l07 import java.math.BigDecimal import java.util.Optional import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService import java.util.concurrent.Executors private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(msg: String) = println("%4d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg)) private fun ask(name: String, ms: Long, price: String?, io: ExecutorService): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ Thread.sleep(ms) if (price == null) { log("$name fails") throw IllegalStateException("$name is closed today") } log("$name answers $price") BigDecimal(price) }, io) /** Three suppliers quote a sack of flour: corner fails at 50 ms, market answers at 100 ms, mill at 300 ms. Pass any, all or safe. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "all" Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> val asks = listOf(ask("corner", 50, null, io), ask("market", 100, "21.50", io), ask("mill", 300, "19.80", io)) val result: CompletableFuture<*> = when (mode) { // the first future to complete wins, even when it completes with a failure "any" -> CompletableFuture.anyOf(*asks.toTypedArray()) // waits for all three, then fails because one of them failed "all" -> CompletableFuture.allOf(*asks.toTypedArray()) .thenApply { asks.map { it.join() }.min() } // turn each failure into an empty Optional first, so allOf can't fail else -> { val safe = asks.map { f -> f.handle { price, ex -> if (ex == null) Optional.of(price) else Optional.empty() } } CompletableFuture.allOf(*safe.toTypedArray()) .thenApply { safe.mapNotNull { it.join().orElse(null) }.min() } } } result.handle { v, ex -> log("$mode: " + if (ex == null) "result $v" else "failed with ${ex.cause}") }.join() } }

try.expect: any fails at about 50 ms with the corner shop's closed today, and the market and the mill keep going after the result is printed. all fails with the same exception, but only at about 300 ms, after the mill answers. safe succeeds at about 300 ms with 19.80, the mill's price, because the failure became an empty Optional. On a busy machine, every timestamp runs a little late.

compare.title: One supplier call with a deadline: CompletableFuture vs coroutines

java.title: Ask.java (CompletableFuture)
java.html: CompletableFuture<Optional<Quote>> ask(QuoteProvider p, String item) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> new Quote(p.name(), p.quote(item)), io) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // the caller stops waiting... .handle((q, ex) -> ex == null ? Optional.of(q) : Optional.empty()); // ...but p.quote keeps running on io until it returns }

kotlin.title: Ask.kt (kotlinx.coroutines)
kotlin.html: suspend fun ask(p: QuoteProvider, item: String): Quote? = try { withTimeoutOrNull(300.milliseconds) { // null when time is up runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { // interrupts the thread on cancel Quote(p.name(), p.quote(item)) } } } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e // never swallow cancellation } catch (e: Exception) { null // a failure becomes "no answer" }

compare.note: Both versions have the same shape: a deadline, then a failure turned into "no answer". The difference is what happens to the work. orTimeout only completes the future, and the supplier call runs to its end. Kotlin's coroutines, its own light tasks with a track of their own, can do more. withTimeoutOrNull cancels the block when time is up, and runInterruptible turns that cancellation into Thread.interrupt() on the IO thread. So a blocking call that responds to interrupts stops and gives its thread back. In both languages, a call that ignores interrupts keeps its thread, which is why the client's own timeout still matters. Kotlin has one trap of its own: when you catch Exception, you must rethrow CancellationException by hand, or the coroutine stops responding to cancellation. CompletableFuture has no such trap.

worked.title: Give the flour price a deadline and a fallback

steps.say: The kitchen gets the flour price from its main supplier through an async client, a library whose methods return a CompletableFuture. When the supplier hangs, everything that needs the price hangs with it. Before reading on, decide what should happen after 300 ms.
steps.code: CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price(String item) { return supplier.priceAsync(item); // no deadline: a hung supplier hangs the kitchen }

alt.html: fun price(item: String): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = supplier.priceAsync(item) // no deadline: a hung supplier hangs the kitchen

steps.say: Give the call a deadline, count failures without changing them, then fall back to a second supplier, which has an async client too. metrics is a small counter that a dashboard reads. The fallback gets a short deadline of its own, because exceptionallyCompose starts a new call that the first timeout doesn't cover.
steps.code: CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price(String item) { return supplier.priceAsync(item) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 1. the main call gets 300 ms .whenComplete((p, ex) -> { // 2. look, don't change if (ex != null) metrics.count("price.failed", unwrap(ex).getClass().getSimpleName()); }) .exceptionallyCompose(ex -> backup.priceAsync(item) // 3. fall back, asynchronously .orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)); // 4. the fallback's own deadline }

alt.html: fun price(item: String): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = supplier.priceAsync(item) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 1. the main call gets 300 ms .whenComplete { _, ex -> // 2. look, don't change if (ex != null) metrics.count("price.failed", unwrap(ex).javaClass.simpleName) } .exceptionallyCompose { // 3. fall back, asynchronously backup.priceAsync(item).orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 4. the fallback's own deadline }

steps.say: Why unwrap in the counter? The supplier's client may complete its future with a bare exception, orTimeout stores a bare TimeoutException, and anything thrown inside a stage arrives in an envelope. Without unwrapping, half the failures would be counted as CompletionException, which tells the person reading the dashboard nothing.

One gap is left. After 300 ms the kitchen moves on, but the main call still holds a thread and a network connection. Give the request a timeout of its own, so the client gives up too. With the JDK's HTTP client, it's one line on the request.
steps.code: HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // 5. the call stops waiting too .build();

lab.title: A price checker that survives bad suppliers
steps: Meet the classes. A QuoteProvider is one supplier's price service: quote(item) makes a blocking call and returns today's price, or throws. A Quote is one answer, the supplier's name and its price. QuoteAggregator.best(item) must ask every supplier at once and complete with the lowest Quote. Its Javadoc is the spec. Run the tests: all seven fail.
Write unwrap: loop while the throwable is a CompletionException or an ExecutionException and has a cause, moving to the cause each time.

Add a private method ask(QuoteProvider p, String item) that returns CompletableFuture<Optional<Quote>>: supplyAsync on io, then orTimeout, then handle. On failure, call onSkip.accept(p.name(), unwrap(ex)) and return Optional.empty().

In best, map every supplier to ask, collect the futures in a list, and pass them to allOf. In the thenApply after it, join each future, keep the quotes that are present, and return the lowest price, or throw NoQuoteException.
Run the tests until all seven pass, then once more.
hints: orTimeout takes a long and a unit: orTimeout(timeout.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).
allOf takes an array (asks.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) and returns CompletableFuture<Void>. Read the quotes from your own list.
If skipsFailingProvider reports a CompletionException, you passed ex to onSkip without unwrapping it. If skipsSlowProvider times out, the deadline is on the whole call, not on each supplier.
Throwing NoQuoteException inside the thenApply is enough: the returned future fails with it as the cause.

drill.title: A price with a deadline and a fallback
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price(String item): call main.priceAsync(item) with a 300 ms deadline. If it fails for any reason, log the unwrapped cause and fall back to backup.priceAsync(item), which returns a CompletableFuture too. Then compare. Which method did you use for the fallback, and did you unwrap before logging?

answer.title: Prices.java
answer.html: CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price(String item) { return main.priceAsync(item) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) .exceptionallyCompose(ex -> { Throwable cause = ex instanceof CompletionException && ex.getCause() != null ? ex.getCause() : ex; log.warn("main supplier failed, asking the backup: {}", cause.toString()); return backup.priceAsync(item); // a future, so exceptionallyCompose, not exceptionally }); }

alt.title: Prices.kt
alt.html: fun price(item: String): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = main.priceAsync(item) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) .exceptionallyCompose { ex -> val cause = if (ex is CompletionException && ex.cause != null) ex.cause!! else ex log.warn("main supplier failed, asking the backup: {}", cause.toString()) backup.priceAsync(item) // a future, so exceptionallyCompose, not exceptionally }

recap: A failure skips every later stage until a handler. exceptionally and handle can recover, whenComplete only looks, and exceptionallyCompose (JDK 12) recovers with another future.
Recover as close to the failure as you can, so that every stage after the handler runs as usual.
An exception thrown inside a stage reaches handlers wrapped in a CompletionException. completeExceptionally and orTimeout store it bare. Unwrap before you test the type.
orTimeout and completeOnTimeout end the caller's wait, not the work, and cancel(true) on a CompletableFuture interrupts nothing. Give the call its own timeout in the client.

allOf waits for every future and fails if any failed. anyOf takes the first to finish, failures included. For a fan-out, give each call its own deadline and turn its failure into "no answer" before allOf.
The limit: a CompletableFuture can stop waiting but can't stop the work, and one failed call doesn't cancel the others. It suits work that waits, not one big pile of arithmetic.

explain.prompt: A friend's price checker does allOf(askCorner, askMarket, askMill).orTimeout(500, MILLISECONDS) and then picks the lowest price. Explain why it fails whenever one supplier is closed or slow, and how you would change it.
explain.answer: allOf fails if any of its futures fails, so one closed supplier fails the whole call, and only after the slowest supplier has finished. The single orTimeout on the allOf means one hung supplier makes the whole call time out and throws away the prices that did come back. I'd give each supplier call its own orTimeout, then a handle that turns a failure into an empty Optional and reports the unwrapped cause. Then allOf over those safe futures can't fail, and the step after it picks the lowest price among the ones that are present, or fails with a clear "no quote" error if all are empty. I'd also set a timeout in the HTTP client, because orTimeout doesn't stop the call itself.

deeper.html:
anyOf gives you the first to finish, not the first to succeed. When you want the first success, complete a future of your own from each success, and fail it only when every call has failed. complete returns false for every caller after the first, so the first success wins without a lock:

Java
static <T> CompletableFuture<T> firstSuccess(List<CompletableFuture<T>> calls) {   // calls must not be empty
    CompletableFuture<T> first = new CompletableFuture<>();
    AtomicInteger failed = new AtomicInteger();
    for (CompletableFuture<T> call : calls) {
        call.whenComplete((value, ex) -> {
            if (ex == null) first.complete(value);                                   // only the first one counts
            else if (failed.incrementAndGet() == calls.size()) first.completeExceptionally(ex);
        });
    }
    return first;
}
Kotlin
fun <T> firstSuccess(calls: List<CompletableFuture<T>>): CompletableFuture<T> {     // calls must not be empty
    val first = CompletableFuture<T>()
    val failed = AtomicInteger()
    for (call in calls) {
        call.whenComplete { value, ex ->
            if (ex == null) first.complete(value)                                    // only the first one counts
            else if (failed.incrementAndGet() == calls.size) first.completeExceptionally(ex)
        }
    }
    return first
}

Two smaller things are worth knowing. orTimeout and completeOnTimeout change the very future you call them on. If a library hands the same cached future to several callers, one caller's timeout fails it for all of them. Call copy() (JDK 9) first, and put the timeout on your copy. And when you need a delay without a timeout, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(500, MILLISECONDS, io) (JDK 9) returns an Executor that runs each task 500 ms after you hand it over. It's handy for a retry that waits a little first: supplyAsync(this::call, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(500, MILLISECONDS, io)).
